explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says the kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken came along (Ruth 4:1). Back on the threshing floor, Boaz told Ruth there was a kinsman-redeemer nearer than he was (Ruth 3:12). Boaz sat down and the very man he needed walked right up to him.

Good memory of the field, baker, but the gate is a different scene. That servant was the one in charge of the harvesters, and he told Boaz about Ruth out in the field (Ruth 2:5-6). At the gate, the man who comes along is the kinsman-redeemer Boaz had spoken of (Ruth 4:1). Different man, different job.

explanations.answer: One of the young men from the field
explanations.explanation: The young men worked Boaz's field, and Boaz had told them not to touch Ruth (Ruth 2:9). The gate is a different scene. The man who comes along is the kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken (Ruth 4:1). That field crew belongs to the harvest story.

That's right, baker. Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and said, "Sit here," and they did so (Ruth 4:2). Ten leaders, all sitting down, and the whole thing is out in the open. That's one witness table you do NOT want to argue with.
This passage doesn't mention any priests. Boaz took ten of the elders of the city (Ruth 4:2). They're the ones he tells to sit at the gate. It's city leaders in those seats.

No soldiers show up in this scene. The text says Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and told them to sit (Ruth 4:2). Nobody needs a sword for this. Just ten seats and a very serious conversation.

Not quite, friend. Boaz says, "…there is no one but you to redeem it, and I am next after you." (Ruth 4:4). So the other man is first in line, and Boaz is second. Boaz stands second in line, and that matters in this story.

You got it, baker. Boaz tells the man, "…there is no one but you to redeem it, and I am next after you." (Ruth 4:4). The other man is first, and Boaz stands right behind him. Boaz is not pushing his way to the front of this line.
That's the one, baker. The man answers, "I will redeem it…" (Ruth 4:4). That is his answer to Boaz about the land. And Boaz has one more thing to say to him next (Ruth 4:5).
Nope, the man doesn't ask for a few days. He answers, "I will redeem it…" (Ruth 4:4). That's a yes to the land, not a maybe.
No family meeting in this scene. The man simply says, "I will redeem it…" (Ruth 4:4). He answers on the spot, right there at the gate. Nothing in the text says he checked with anybody.

explanations.answer: Acquire the widow of the deceased
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Boaz says that on the day he buys the land from Naomi and Ruth the Moabitess, he must also acquire the widow of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance (Ruth 4:5). So the land comes with Ruth, and that changes the whole deal. Boaz laid it out plainly, no fine print.

explanations.answer: Pay the debts of the deceased
explanations.explanation: Debts aren't mentioned at the gate. Boaz says the man must also acquire the widow of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance (Ruth 4:5). That's the catch, and it's about Ruth, not a bill. Good guess, though, because bills ruin plenty of good days.

explanations.answer: Repair the house of the deceased
explanations.explanation: No repair work in this deal, baker. Boaz says the man must also acquire the widow of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance (Ruth 4:5). The text doesn't mention a house needing fixes. No hammers, just a widow and a name.

Not anymore, friend. Once Boaz mentions the widow, the man says, "I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance." (Ruth 4:6). He had said yes to the land, and then he backs out. The deal changed, and so did his answer.

That's right, baker. The man says, "I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance." (Ruth 4:6). Earlier he had said, "I will redeem it…" (Ruth 4:4), and then Boaz added Ruth to the deal (Ruth 4:5). Once Ruth is part of the deal, his answer changes.

explanations.answer: It would jeopardize his own inheritance
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. He says, "I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance." (Ruth 4:6). That's the reason he gives, and the text gives no other. So he steps aside and asks Boaz to take his right of redemption.

explanations.answer: He can't afford the price Naomi is asking
explanations.explanation: Price never comes up at the gate. The man gives one reason: "…I would jeopardize my own inheritance." (Ruth 4:6). Nothing in the text says Naomi named a price or that money was his problem. I'd stick to what he actually said.

explanations.answer: He already has too many fields to work
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about his fields being full. His one stated reason is that he "…would jeopardize my own inheritance." (Ruth 4:6). I know a full to-do list is a believable excuse, but he didn't use it. Stick with the words he said.

That's it, baker. He removes his sandal and tells Boaz, "Buy it for yourself." (Ruth 4:8). That hands the right of redemption over to Boaz. And that sandal is the confirmation, since in former times in Israel a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party to make a matter legally binding (Ruth 4:7).
No sharing plans here. The man hands over his sandal and says, "Buy it for yourself." (Ruth 4:8). He steps out of the deal entirely. Boaz gets it on his own.

The man doesn't pass it to some third person. He tells Boaz, "Buy it for yourself." (Ruth 4:8). Boaz was already next after him, so the right goes straight to Boaz (Ruth 4:4). One sandal, one handoff, done.

That's right, baker. Boaz says to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon." (Ruth 4:9). Elimelech was Naomi's husband, and Chilion and Mahlon were their sons (Ruth 1:2). Boaz is calling in the whole crowd as witnesses, and that is a big, public yes.

This one is true, friend. Boaz says to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon." (Ruth 4:9). Elimelech, Naomi's husband, and his sons Chilion and Mahlon all get named (Ruth 1:2). All three names are in what Boaz says to the crowd.

Right on, baker. Boaz says he has acquired Ruth "…so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home." (Ruth 4:10). The name in question is Mahlon's, Ruth's late husband. Boaz is making sure that name stays standing.

Flocks never come up in Boaz's announcement. He says he is acquiring Ruth "…so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home." (Ruth 4:10). It's about the name of the deceased. Sheep stay out of this one.

Servants aren't in this part of the announcement. Boaz says he is acquiring Ruth "…so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home." (Ruth 4:10). What he wants kept alive is the name of the deceased. Nobody's hiring here.

That's right, baker. The people at the gate say, "May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel." (Ruth 4:11). They are sisters, and both were wives of Jacob (Genesis 29:23, 28). That's a big name to say over Ruth, and the whole gate said it.

Good names, but not the ones the crowd said. Sarah was Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:15), and Rebekah was Isaac's wife (Genesis 24:67). The people at the gate named "…Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel." (Ruth 4:11). Same family story, but a different pair of women.

Strong women, but not who the crowd picked. Miriam was a prophetess, Aaron's sister (Exodus 15:20), and Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel (Judges 4:4). The people at the gate said "…Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel." (Ruth 4:11). Those two are the pair the crowd wanted for Ruth.

You got it, baker. The crowd wishes that Boaz's house may become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, "…because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman." (Ruth 4:12). Offspring is the word they use.

Long life isn't what they mention. The crowd says "…because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman." (Ruth 4:12). That's about children. I'd call that a good wish, but not the one they said.

Wisdom isn't in their blessing. The crowd wishes that Boaz's house may become like the house of Perez "…because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman." (Ruth 4:12). The word they name is offspring, not wisdom. Wisdom's a fine thing to ask for, but it's not the one they name.
Yes, baker. The text says that when Boaz had relations with Ruth, "…the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son." (Ruth 4:13). The text credits the LORD for it. A son is born.

This one is true, friend. The text says "…the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son." (Ruth 4:13). So a baby boy is born, and the text says the LORD enabled it. The crowd's blessing at the gate had spoken of the offspring the LORD will give Boaz by Ruth (Ruth 4:12).

That's right, baker. The women say, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer." (Ruth 4:14). They are speaking to Naomi, and they start by blessing the LORD. After her hard words earlier (Ruth 1:20-21), that is a big turn for her.

Elders were at the gate for the deal, but that's not what the women say here. They say the LORD "…has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer." (Ruth 4:14). That's the word they use for Naomi. A kinsman-redeemer is the key piece.

No servant in this blessing. The women say, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer." (Ruth 4:14). Naomi isn't being handed a helper. The word they pick is kinsman-redeemer.

explanations.answer: Sustain her in her old age
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The women say, "He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age." (Ruth 4:15). They're telling Naomi this about the baby. Renew her life and sustain her. That's a lot to put on one little guy.

Naomi already came back from Moab, and she came to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:22). The women don't say anything about going back. They say, "He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age." (Ruth 4:15). The promise is about renewing her life and sustaining her, not a trip.

A house isn't in what they say. The women tell Naomi, "He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age." (Ruth 4:15). That's what they say the baby will do. The text names sustaining her, not construction.
That's right, baker. The women say Naomi's daughter-in-law "…loves you and is better to you than seven sons…" (Ruth 4:15). That is a big compliment. Seven sons is the number they name.

This one is true, friend. The women say Naomi's daughter-in-law "…loves you and is better to you than seven sons…" (Ruth 4:15). They name the love, and they name the number seven. That is high praise for Ruth.
Right, baker. The text says, "…Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him." (Ruth 4:16). The baby is right there in her lap. After all that, I think she held on tight.

This one is true, friend. The text says, "…Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him." (Ruth 4:16). So Naomi holds the baby and cares for him. That's the scene the text gives us.

Not this time, friend. The text says the neighbor women "…named him Obed." (Ruth 4:17). Boaz and Ruth aren't the ones naming him. The neighbor women say, "A son has been born to Naomi…" and then they give the name.

That's right, baker. The neighbor women are the ones who say, "A son has been born to Naomi…" and they named him Obed (Ruth 4:17). So the naming comes from the neighbors. The text doesn't say Boaz or Ruth did it.

That's the one, baker. Ruth 4:17 says Obed "…became the father of Jesse, the father of David." David later became king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). The book ends by tracing the line from Perez down to David (Ruth 4:18-22).

Samuel is part of David's story, since he anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13), but he isn't the one this line names. The text says Obed "…became the father of Jesse, the father of David." (Ruth 4:17). Samuel isn't named in this family list. Good name, but not the one this list gives.

Solomon was David's son (2 Samuel 12:24), so he comes after the name we need. The text says Obed "…became the father of Jesse, the father of David." (Ruth 4:17). You jumped one generation ahead, baker. The man we want is Jesse's son, David.
